The previous step's state arrives as a texture, iChannel0. To read what was at this very pixel: texture2D(iChannel0, fragCoord / iResolution.xy). For the neighbour to the right, you add one pixel: (fragCoord + vec2(1.0, 0.0)) / iResolution.xy.

What the shader returns in color is the new state, which on the next step will come back in. The four channels can be used as four state numbers, not necessarily as colours.

The method is only stable if $\alpha \le \frac{1}{4}$. With a larger value, the finest possible pattern, a chessboard of heat and cold, is multiplied at each step by $1 - 8\alpha$, which is less than $-1$, and grows out of control. It is the same stability as that of [[av-edo-numerico|Euler's method]].
En [[gfx-tiempo]] quedó escrita una regl: In [[gfx-tiempo]] a rule was set down: a shader does not remember the previous frame. All movement is a formula of time. This topic breaks that rule. With a simple trick — painting into an invisible image and reading it on the next frame — the shader can compute each frame from the previous one.

La [[av-edp|ecuación del calor]] dice qu: The [[av-edp|heat equation]] says that the temperature at a point changes according to how different it is from the average of its surroundings: if the neighbours are hotter, it rises; if they are colder, it falls. Discretised on a grid, it is a local rule of the kind a shader runs effortlessly.

La idea de simular física en la tarjeta: The idea of simulating physics on the graphics card was born almost as a trick. In the early 2000s, when shaders started to be programmable, several researchers realised that painting into a texture and reading it back was a way of doing parallel computation with a device meant for video games. That way fluids, smoke and chemical reactions were simulated far faster than on the processor. Out of that habit came general-purpose computing on graphics cards, which today supports a good part of scientific simulation and the training of neural networks.
